skill.name: Same story, another character's eyes
skill.why: Every story has two sides. Swapping eyes makes old stories new again.
skill.how: Pick a side character. Retell the story as 'I', with their thoughts and feelings.

steps.say: Little Red Riding Hood: a girl visits Gran. A wolf gets there first and dresses up as Gran.

show.text: The wolf ran to Gran's house and jumped into her bed.

options.reason: Does the wolf say I or my? Look again.
Gran doesn't say anything. Is there an I in it?

steps.win: Right. Nobody says I. We just watch from the outside. That is the usual way.

steps.say: In a game, you can swap players. Stories can swap too. Now the wolf tells it.

show.nudge: That's where he went. Which word shows the wolf is telling it?
Her means Gran. Find the word the wolf uses for himself.

steps.ask: Tap the word that shows the wolf is telling it.
steps.win: Yes! I. The wolf tells his own story now. Telling it as I is called first person.

steps.say: Saying I is not enough. Readers want to know what the wolf thinks and feels.

show.nudge: That's what he did. Which part shows how he feels?
That's another action. Which part shows how he feels?

show.text: Honestly, I was so hungry I felt dizzy.

steps.ask: Tap the part that shows how the wolf feels.
steps.win: Yes! Now we know what it's like to be him. His thoughts and feelings make it his story.

steps.say: Careful. The wolf can only tell what he sees, hears and thinks. One line breaks that.

show.nudge: The wolf knows this. He's the one hiding!

show.text: At home, Red's mum was baking.

show.nudge: That's the wolf's own tummy. He knows how he feels.

steps.ask: Tap the line the wolf could NOT know.
steps.win: Yes! The wolf wasn't at Red's house. He can't know what her mum was doing.

steps.say: Now Gran tells it. But lots of lines say I. Check who the I is, and where they are.
steps.ask: Which line is told through Gran's eyes?

options.text: I knocked, and an old lady opened the door.
options.reason: Who did the knocking? That I is outside the door, not Gran.

options.text: I heard a knock, and a hairy voice said, 'It's me, Gran!'
Gran opened the door and screamed.
options.reason: Nobody says I here. We're watching Gran from outside.

steps.win: Yes! Gran is inside, hearing the knock. Saying I isn't enough. Check who the I is.

steps.say: The Tortoise and the Hare: a fast hare naps in a race. A slow tortoise wins.
steps.ask: Which first line tells it through the hare's eyes?

options.text: The hare lay down under a tree and slept.
options.reason: Nobody says I. We're watching the hare from outside.

options.text: I plodded on, slow and steady, past the sleeping hare.
options.reason: This I walks past the sleeping hare. That's the tortoise!

options.text: I only shut my eyes for one minute. One!

steps.win: Yes! It's I, it's the hare, and you can hear how cross he is. Now pick your character.

terms.means: The character telling the story. They say I, me and my.
What the teller thinks and feels.
Something your teller didn't see, hear or think. Leave it out.
Nobody in the story says I. We watch from outside.

examples.text: Honestly, I was so hungry I felt dizzy.
Then a goat ate my daisies, and nobody cared.

card.test: Who is the I? Did they see it, hear it or think it? If not, cut it.

weDo.frame: Zed is retelling The Three Little Pigs for story night.
weDo.prompt: Which sentence is told through the wolf's eyes?
weDo.hint: Who is saying I, and where are they standing?
weDo.success: The wolf says I and gives his own side, so we see the story through his eyes.

options.text: I knocked politely on all three doors, but somehow I'm the villain.
The wolf huffed and puffed and blew the house down.
options.reason: This is told from the outside, about the wolf. Nobody says I.

options.text: I watched from my brick house as the wolf ran away.
options.reason: This uses I, but it's a pig speaking from inside the brick house.

weDo.frame: Zed is retelling Jack and the Beanstalk, but his pages got mixed up.
weDo.prompt: Put each line with the character whose eyes we're seeing through.
weDo.hint: Ask: whose house is it, and whose hen?
weDo.success: Clues like 'my hen' and 'tiny thief' belong to the giant. Climbing and tiptoeing belong to Jack.

items.text: I've never climbed this high. My legs won't stop shaking.
items.reason: Jack is the one who climbs the beanstalk, so these are his shaking legs.

items.text: A tiny thief has run off with my hen!
items.reason: The hen belongs to the giant, so 'my hen' is his voice.

items.text: Someone has left muddy little footprints on my kitchen table.
items.reason: It's the giant's kitchen, and Jack's footprints look little to him.

items.text: Mum is going to be so proud of me.
items.reason: Jack's mum is waiting at home at the bottom of the beanstalk.

items.text: The giant's snores shake the castle as I tiptoe past.
items.reason: The person tiptoeing past the giant is the visitor: Jack.

creature.name: Peerlet
creature.blurb: A moth with a big eyespot on each wing. Each eye sees the same night differently, and it loves hearing both sides.

workshop.mentor: Let me tell you about my bridge. I built it myself, stone by stone, and I keep it spotless. I sweep it every morning. I even planted daisies along the edge. Then one day: trip, trap, trip, trap. A goat. A small goat, chewing my daisies with his mouth open. I asked him, very politely, to stop. He said his big brother would deal with me. Then the next brother came, and ate the rest of my daisies. And then the biggest one turned up, and nobody, NOBODY, ever asks what happened to me after that. I'll tell you what happened. I've been living in a drain ever since, and the goats got a bridge for free.
workshop.ask: Retell a story through another character's eyes. Ideas: the giant from Jack and the Beanstalk, Maxx during a heist, the losing hare, the footy in a grand final.
checklist: I wrote as 'I', from one character's eyes.
I kept the main events of the story.
I showed what my character thinks and feels.
I only told what my character could know.
